92.title: Manna (Exodus 16)
92.hook: bread from heaven, enough for each day, and a double portion before Shabbat
92.howItsDone: Jews recall the manna every Shabbat with two loaves of challah on the table, and some say a reading about the manna in daily prayers as a lesson in trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miriam's timbrel, the drum the women packed before there was anything to celebrate. Your line was bring the drum. Now the food runs out.

Open a fridge and look at it the way a desert traveler would. Leftovers in the back you forgot about. Three kinds of mustard. A lot of us stock up, just in case, because tomorrow feels uncertain. A month out of Egypt, the Israelites are in the wilderness, and the food from Egypt has run out. They complain: back in Egypt we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill. And God answers with a strange promise: bread will fall from the sky every morning. But you can only take enough for today.
screen: `THE FOOD RUNS OUT.` → `BACK IN EGYPT WE ATE OUR FILL.` → `BREAD FROM THE SKY, ONE DAY AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: God says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Behold, I will cause to rain bread from heaven for you." Next morning the dew lifts, and on the ground there's something fine and flaky, like frost. The people say to each other, man hu? What is it? "For they knew not what it was." The name sticks: man, manna, is basically the word what. They ate a question for forty years. The Torah says it was white, like coriander seed, and tasted like wafers made with honey. The rabbis added that it tasted like whatever each person wanted. Now the rules. Each person gathers about an omer, a measure of a day's food. Some gather more, some less, and when they measure it, nobody has too much and nobody too little. Don't keep any until morning. Some people do anyway, and by morning it's full of worms and stinks. Except for one day. On the sixth day, everyone finds twice as much, and the extra keeps overnight, because on the seventh day nothing falls. So in the wilderness the people keep a Shabbat, and it comes with a double portion. Tradition links that to the two loaves on the Shabbat table today; more on them later. The rabbis saw manna as a daily school of trust. You couldn't hoard it. You had to go out each morning and find there was enough, again. Moses later puts it this way: people don't live by bread alone. And a jar of manna, the story says, was kept for future generations to see.

segments.voice: Think of one thing you tend to over-gather: food, clothes, tabs open on your phone, worry about next week. Hold it up to the manna rule, enough for today and no more, and ask what enough looks like, just for today. Then set the rest down for now, like a bag you've been carrying for no reason.
Manna. From man hu, what is it? Bread from heaven, gathered each morning, enough for one day, and double before Shabbat.

93.title: Jethro's advice (Exodus 18)
93.hook: Moses' father-in-law tells him he can't judge everyone alone
93.howItsDone: Parashat Yitro, which includes Jethro's visit and the Ten Commandments, is read in synagogue each winter as part of the yearly Torah cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna: bread from heaven, gathered one morning at a time. Your line was enough for today. Now a visitor comes to the camp.

At some workplaces there's one person who answers every question, signs off on every decision, stays late every night, and is quietly falling apart. Or the parent who does all of it because it's faster than explaining. In the wilderness, Moses is that person. From morning until evening, a line of people stands in front of him, waiting for him to settle their arguments. Then his father-in-law comes to visit, watches for one day, and says something very plain.
screen: `THE ONE WHO DOES IT ALL.` → `A LINE FROM MORNING TO EVENING.` → `THE FATHER-IN-LAW WATCHES.`

segments.voice: Jethro, Yitro in Hebrew, is a priest of Midian, not an Israelite. Moses married his daughter Zipporah years before, when he ran away from Egypt. Now Jethro hears everything God did for the people. He comes out to the desert, brings Moses's wife and sons, and rejoices with him. The next morning he watches Moses work, and asks: why are you sitting alone, with everyone standing around you from morning to evening? Moses says, they come to me to ask of God, and I judge between them. Jethro answers, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The thing that thou doest is not good." You'll wear yourself out, you and the people with you, "for the thing is too heavy for thee; thou art not able to perform it thyself alone." Then he gives him a plan. Teach everyone the laws, so they know the way. Find capable people who fear God, love truth and hate a bribe. Put them in charge of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them handle the small cases, and bring you only the hard ones. And Moses, the man who spoke with God at the burning bush, listens to his father-in-law and does all of it. A detail the tradition keeps: the Torah portion that holds the Ten Commandments is named Yitro, after an outsider. Good advice, it suggests, can come from outside the camp. A whole system of judges began with someone saying, gently, you can't do this alone.

segments.voice: Picture the line of things waiting for you this week, the way Moses saw a line of people, and walk down it slowly. 94.title: The mountain (Exodus 19–20)
94.hook: thunder, a shofar, the whole people at the foot of Sinai; the rabbis say every Jewish soul was there
94.tomorrow: the calf and the second tablets
94.howItsDone: Jews celebrate the giving of the Torah on Shavuot, seven weeks after Passover, when the Ten Commandments are read aloud in synagogue and many stay up all night studying.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jethro's advice: the work is too heavy for one. Your line was you can't carry it alone.

A huge crowd going quiet at once. A stadium during a moment of silence. A candlelight vigil. Tens of thousands of people, and you can hear a coat rustle. Three months after leaving Egypt, the people camp at the foot of a mountain in the desert. For three days they get ready: they wash their clothes, they wait, and a boundary is set around the mountain. On the third morning, the sky breaks open.
screen: `A HUGE CROWD GOES QUIET.` → `THREE DAYS OF GETTING READY.` → `ON THE THIRD MORNING.`

segments.voice: Thunder. Lightning. A thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of a shofar, a ram's horn, growing louder. The mountain smokes like a furnace, and it shakes. The whole people trembles. Then God speaks the words Jews call aseret hadibrot, the Ten Words, which English calls the Ten Commandments. I am the LORD thy God, who brought you out of Egypt. Have no other gods. Remember the Sabbath. Honor your father and mother. Do not murder, steal, lie, or covet. Then comes a line that has puzzled readers ever since. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And all the people perceived the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the voice of the horn." In Hebrew, the verb is ro'im, they saw. They saw the voices. The rabbis took it literally: at Sinai, people saw what is usually heard. A midrash adds that when God spoke, no bird sang, no ox lowed, the sea didn't stir. The whole world went silent to listen. Then a teaching you first met on day ten: who was there? The Torah later says the covenant was made not only with those standing there that day, but also with those who were not there. The rabbis read that to mean every Jewish soul, every future generation, and every person who would one day choose to become Jewish, stood at the foot of the mountain. That's why many Jews tell the story in the first person: we stood at Sinai. It isn't a memory of ancestors. It's a place you were. And the people's answer, a few chapters later, became famous too: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey."

segments.voice: The midrash says the whole world went still at Sinai, so try a small version for a minute: let the sounds around you come in, a fridge, a car, a bird, your own breath, without naming them. Then, underneath them, listen for the quiet. If you pray, you might listen for what the quiet is saying; if you don't, just rest in it.
The mountain. Sinai, where the people stood in thunder and silence and heard the Ten Words, and where, the rabbis say, every soul was present.
Your line: everyone was there. Whoever you meet stood at that mountain too, the old idea says. Day ninety-four, done.

screen: `DAY 94 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CALF AND THE SECOND TABLETS.`

95.title: The calf and the second tablets (Exodus 32–34)
95.hook: the covenant breaks, the tablets shatter, new ones are carved; the Talmud says both were kept in the ark (Berakhot 8b)
95.carry: the broken tablets were kept too
95.howItsDone: The Thirteen Attributes of Mercy from Exodus 34 are sung in synagogue on festivals, fast days and throughout Yom Kippur, which tradition links to the day the second tablets came down.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mountain: thunder, a shofar, and a whole people who heard the Ten Words. Your line was everyone was there. Then Moses goes up, and stays.

A drawer, a shoebox, a folder on a laptop: plenty of homes keep one, full of things that are broken but can't be thrown away. A cracked mug from a grandparent. A letter from a friendship that ended. A cast from a broken arm. Moses has been up the mountain for forty days, and the people below decide he isn't coming back. What happens next breaks the covenant almost as soon as it's made. And at the end of it, something broken ends up in the ark itself.
screen: `A BOX OF BROKEN THINGS.` → `FORTY DAYS, AND NO MOSES.` → `THE COVENANT BREAKS.`

segments.voice: The people panic and go to Aaron: make us a god to lead us. He collects their gold earrings, and a golden calf comes out of the fire. They bring offerings, eat, drink and dance. On the mountain, God tells Moses what's happening. Moses comes down carrying two stone tablets, written, the Torah says, by the finger of God. He sees the calf and the dancing, throws the tablets down, and they shatter at the foot of the mountain. It's a terrible scene, and the Torah doesn't soften it. Then Moses goes back up and pleads for the people, and the story turns. God reveals a description of divine mercy that synagogues still sing on fast days and holy days, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." And God says: "Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first." This time Moses carves the stones himself. Jewish tradition says he came down with the second tablets on the tenth of Tishrei, the day that became Yom Kippur, the day of forgiveness. Now the Talmud's surprise. What happened to the broken pieces? You'd expect them to be swept away. Instead, the Talmud teaches that the whole tablets and the broken tablets were placed together in the ark of the covenant. And it draws a lesson: honor an elder who has forgotten their learning, because the broken tablets were kept in the ark too. What broke is not thrown out. It travels with what was made new.
screen: `THE GOLDEN CALF.` · `THE TABLETS SHATTER.` · `MERCIFUL AND GRACIOUS.` · `BOTH KEPT IN THE ARK.` · then, large: `HEW THEE TWO TABLES OF STONE.`

segments.voice: Think of something broken in your life: an object, a friendship, a plan, a part of your health, a person who isn't who they used to be. Don't fix it now; just give it a place, setting it down gently beside the things that are whole, in the same box. If a person came to mind, think of one way to honor them.
Shivrei luchot, Hebrew for the broken tablets: kept in the ark beside the new ones when the covenant was renewed.
Your line: the broken tablets were kept too. What broke still rides in the ark. See you tomorrow.

96.title: Camp 2 close: the tabernacle (Exodus 35–40)
96.hook: Exodus ends with a portable dwelling built from everyone's gifts
96.howItsDone: The building of the mishkan is read in synagogue in the last portions of Exodus, and many Jews see each synagogue and each home table as a small sanctuary in its line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shivrei luchot: the broken pieces went into the ark beside the new ones. Your line was the broken tablets were kept too. Today is the last day of camp two.

A potluck is a strange kind of feast: somebody brings the table, somebody brings the chairs, and somebody brings the extension cord nobody remembered. It belongs to everyone because everyone brought a piece. The book of Exodus could have ended with thunder on the mountain. It doesn't. Its last chapters are about a building project in the desert: a tent, made of gifts, that could be folded up and carried. The mishkan, the dwelling.
screen: `EVERYONE BRINGS A PIECE.` → `NOT THUNDER. A BUILDING PROJECT.` → `A TENT YOU CAN CARRY.`

segments.voice: The instruction comes in one line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." Later commentators pointed out that it doesn't say in it. It says among them. The building is for the people. Moses asks for gifts from everyone whose heart moves them: gold, silver, copper, blue and purple and scarlet yarn, linen, goats' hair, wood, oil, spices. Women spin the goats' hair. The women who served at the tent's entrance give their copper mirrors for the washing basin. An artist named Bezalel, filled, the text says, with wisdom and skill, leads the work. Then something happens that fundraisers can only dream of: the people bring too much. The craftsmen tell Moses, and Moses sends word through the camp to stop giving. The word mishkan comes from the root shachan, to dwell, the same root as Shekhinah, the word Jews use for God's presence dwelling close by. And Exodus ends with that presence arriving: a cloud covers the tent, "and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." When the cloud lifted, the people traveled. When it stayed, they stayed. So camp two ends here, after seventy-five days of stories: the voice at the beginning, the garden, Cain and Abel, Noah and the rainbow, Babel, Abraham going forth, Sarah laughing, Jacob wrestling, Joseph and his brothers, the midwives, the bush, the plagues, the sea, the mountain, the calf. It started with a world made by words. It ends with people building a small place for God to live among them, out of whatever they had.

segments.voice: Let one story from this camp stay with you. Then think of something shared you belong to: a family, a building, a team, a congregation, a street. Choose one small thing you could bring to it, an hour, a skill, a dish, a thank-you note, a few dollars, the way the people chose their gifts: because your heart moved you.
Mishkan. The dwelling, the tabernacle, a portable home for God's presence, built from everyone's gifts. Camp two, complete.

97.title: Holy time, not holy place
97.hook: Shabbat is built in time; it begins at sundown on Friday and ends at nightfall Saturday
97.howItsDone: Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday and ends when three stars appear on Saturday night; many Jewish families mark it with candles, a festive meal and a day set apart from work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mishkan, a dwelling built from everyone's gifts, and the end of camp two. Your line was build a place, presence comes. Today camp three begins: the practices.

People cross oceans to stand somewhere holy. A cathedral. A mountaintop. A shrine at the end of a long road. Jewish tradition also keeps a holy place you don't travel to at all, because it travels to you. It arrives every week, on the same day, wherever you are: a hospital room, a dorm, a kitchen in a small apartment. You can't buy a ticket to it, and you can't be too far away from it. It just comes, at sundown, on Friday.
screen: `HOLY PLACES YOU TRAVEL TO.` → `A HOLY PLACE THAT COMES TO YOU.` → `EVERY FRIDAY, AT SUNDOWN.`

segments.voice: Go back to the first chapters of Genesis. God makes light, sky, sea, land, stars, animals and people, and calls them good. But the first thing the Torah calls holy isn't any of them. It's a day. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Hallowed means made holy, kadosh in Hebrew. Before there was a holy mountain or a holy tent, there was a holy time. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel built a whole book on that observation. He described Shabbat as a sanctuary built in time instead of in space, a palace people enter once a week and leave at the end of the day. Yesterday's mishkan was a tent you could carry. Shabbat is even more portable. The Jewish day starts in the evening, because Genesis says there was evening and there was morning. So Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday. Candles are lit a little before sunset, and it ends on Saturday night when three stars can be seen in the sky. A little more than a full day. In that time, observant Jews stop the kind of work that makes and changes the world, and spend the day on rest, meals, prayer, family, study and friends. Others keep parts of it: a Friday dinner, candles, an unplugged afternoon. Jewish movements differ on how Shabbat is kept, and Jews find their own places on that range. What they share is the idea underneath: some things can't be made in space. They can only be kept in time.

segments.voice: Look at the week ahead like a calendar on the wall, and find one hour, Friday night, Saturday afternoon, or any hour that works for your life, to spend without producing, fixing, buying or posting anything. 98.title: Getting ready
98.hook: Friday is for cooking, cleaning and washing, as if a guest were coming
98.howItsDone: In many Jewish homes, Friday is spent cooking the Shabbat meals in advance, cleaning, setting a festive table, bathing and dressing up before candle lighting at sundown.

segments.voice: Yesterday, holy time: the first thing called holy was a day. Your line was a palace in time. That ends a week that ran from manna and Jethro to the mountain, the calf, the mishkan and Shabbat.

One hour before guests arrive, the vacuum comes out. Someone shoves mail into a drawer. The good towels go in the bathroom. Somebody's in the shower, somebody's stirring a pot, and the house smells like onions and soap. It's chaos, and it's also a kind of love. In homes that keep Shabbat, that's Friday afternoon, week after week. Someone important is coming at sundown, and the someone is a day.
screen: `AN HOUR BEFORE THE GUESTS.` → `ONIONS AND SOAP.` → `THE GUEST IS A DAY.`

segments.voice: Erev means evening, or eve. Erev Shabbat is Friday, especially Friday afternoon. The roots go back to the manna. On the sixth day, the Torah says, the people gathered twice as much and prepared what they brought in, so there'd be food on the seventh. Getting ready is built into the very first Shabbat. The Talmud tells how the great rabbis spent Friday, and they weren't too important for chores. One singed the head of an animal for cooking. Another salted a fish. Another cut beets; another carried loads in and out of the house. They did it themselves, on purpose, because honoring Shabbat with your own hands was part of it. And as the sun went down, one sage would wrap himself in his cloak, stand, and say: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the queen. Another would say: come in, O bride. Centuries later, a Friday night song welcoming the Sabbath bride grew from those words. So in many homes, Friday's list goes something like this: cook the meals, because Shabbat has no cooking; clean; set the table with a white cloth; bathe; put on something nice; turn off whatever needs turning off. Some people get ready for hours. Some just do one thing. Either way, it's the idea behind any dinner party. When a guest you love is coming, you don't wait until they're at the door to get ready.
